cf.title: Add pg_stat_log_messages: cumulative statistics about server log messages (was: Add contrib module pg_stat_log: cumulative statistics about server log messages)

input.subject: Add contrib module pg_stat_log: cumulative statistics about server log messages

verdict_reasoning: The goal has support in the thread and a concrete alerting use case, so level 1b does not stop the review. The design does: a fixed shared table that any role can fill (security-1, maintenance-fit-2) can drop the XX001 counts the proposal is justified by. The choice of a fixed-amount kind with a private hash table (maintenance-fit-1) and the log_min_messages floor (standards-compat-1) also need agreement before code review. Bertrand Drouvot's per-backend suggestion is still open.

brief.title: Cumulative statistics view counting server log messages by SQLSTATE
brief.problem: Counting errors by SQLSTATE, database and user today requires parsing the server log, which is costly and lost after rotation. Monitoring roles often get pg_monitor but not log access, because logs can hold statements and sensitive data. Alerting on codes such as XX000, XX001 or XX002 has no counter source.
brief.proposed_design: v2 adds a builtin fixed-amount stats kind, PGSTAT_KIND_LOGMSG, counted in EmitErrorReport() when a message reaches the server log. Entries are keyed by backend type, database, user, elevel and SQLSTATE in an index-based hash table inside the stats block. The table has a compile-time size of 64 entries per named errcode, and new combinations beyond capacity go to a dropped counter.
user_visible_surface: New view pg_stat_log_messages (backend_type, database, user, elevel, sqlerrcode, sqlerrcode_name, count, stats_reset), readable with pg_read_all_stats.
New enum GUC track_log_messages that sets the minimum severity to count; default none.
New function pg_stat_get_log_messages_dropped() reports combinations lost to a full table.
Stats file grows by about 0.6 MB; counters persist across clean restart and are discarded after crash recovery.
author_claims: Overhead in a log storm with many distinct SQLSTATEs was in the low single digits percent; the harness and numbers are not posted.
Workloads that do not log see no measurable overhead.
About 16,800 entries use about 0.6 MB of shared memory, allocated at startup even when tracking is off.
The design complements Joe Conway's 2023 pg_stat_logmsg, which keyed messages by source location.
v1 went through review and adversarial testing as an external extension.
brief.thread_state: Kirk Wolak and Nikolay Samokhvalov support the idea, and Daniel Gustafsson's objection to contrib led to the v2 rewrite into core. Bertrand Drouvot suggests per-backend counters on the redesigned per-backend stats infrastructure; no one has reviewed v2 in detail, and it needs a rebase.
unclear: No benchmark numbers or harness are posted for either version.
The proposal does not say what happens when the server log is not reached, for example with log_min_messages above the tracked level.
The proposal does not say how the table copes with high-cardinality users or databases filling 64 slots per errcode.
The proposal does not say whether counting adds lock contention in EmitErrorReport() under concurrent error storms, or which lock it takes.
The thread does not settle whether per-backend statistics should be part of this design.
Behaviour for messages sent only to the client, not the server log, is not described beyond the log_min_messages floor.

prior_attempts.title: pg_stat_logmsg
prior_attempts.quote: The patch shares a lot of perks with pg_stat_statements that don't scale well.
prior_attempts.reason: The patch did not change after September 2023. In July 2024 reviewers asked what blocked it, questioned whether it belongs in contrib, and pointed out that line numbers change between minor releases, so old and new entries mix after an upgrade. Michael Paquier suggested building on the proposed pluggable cumulative statistics instead of copying the pg_stat_statements design, which does not scale well. The author agreed to put the version in the key and to rework the patch, but said time was the main blocker, and the visible messages show no new version before the entry was closed.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: v2 keys by SQLSTATE, database, user and backend type, which stay stable across minor releases, unlike file name and line number. It is a builtin cumulative stats kind in core, not a contrib module that copies the pg_stat_statements design.

prior_attempts.title: SQL statements statistics counter view (pg_stat_sql)
prior_attempts.quote:
This patch had no activity for months, so I am marking it as returned
with feedback.
prior_attempts.reason: Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback after months without activity, after Alvaro Herrera asked who would rebase it onto the new cmdtaglist.h enum tags. Andres Freund's 2017 review had left open questions: an extension might be the better place, tags should be enums in a fixed array, and counting belongs at the executor level. The author promised an array version, but the visible messages do not show one. A competing cmdstats patch by Mark Dilger also waited on benchmarks that Robert Haas requested.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 counted SQL statements by command tag, not log messages by SQLSTATE. Both add a core counter view behind a track GUC.

objections.title: Unprivileged users can fill the shared table and hide later corruption errors
objections.failure_scenario: Any role runs a PL/pgSQL loop that raises errors with thousands of distinct made-up SQLSTATEs using raise ... using errcode. The fixed table of about 16,800 entries fills, and a later XX001 from another database lands only in the dropped counter. The operator finds out after the corruption, when the expected alert never fired.
objections.argument: Message #4 justifies core placement with alerting on XX000, XX001 and XX002. Message #5 sizes the table as one shared pool, keeps it full until a privileged reset, and lets new combinations fall into a single dropped counter. Raising an error with any SQLSTATE needs no privilege, so a non-privileged role controls what occupies the table. The dropped counter shows that something was lost, but not what.
objections.author_must_show: How does the design keep built-in error classes such as XX countable when a non-privileged role floods the table with user-defined SQLSTATEs?

critic.reasoning: Any role can raise errors with arbitrary SQLSTATEs, and ERROR reaches the server log by default. Message #5 describes one shared pool that stays full until a privileged reset, so the scenario works once tracking is on.

objections.title: A full table can drop the corruption errors the feature exists for
objections.failure_scenario: A multi-tenant cluster with thousands of roles records 28P01 and 42501 per role until all 16,800 slots are used. Weeks later an XX001 arrives, goes only into pg_stat_get_log_messages_dropped(), and the XX001 alert from message #4 never fires. The operator learns of this only after reading the logs.
objections.argument: Message #5 removed v1's max_entries GUC, so an operator cannot raise the capacity without rebuilding. The key includes user and database, so cardinality grows with roles and databases, while the size grows only with the number of SQLSTATE codes. The dropped counter shows that something was lost but not which SQLSTATE. Message #4 gives XX000, XX001 and XX002 alerting as the main use case.
objections.author_must_show: How does the design make sure rare high-severity SQLSTATEs are always counted on clusters with many roles or databases, without a rebuild?

critic.reasoning: The key includes user and database while capacity is fixed at compile time, and message #5 removed max_entries. The v1 example shows 28P01 with no user, so that part of the scenario is weak, but 42501 per role still fills the table.

objections.title: A private hash table inside a fixed-amount stats kind
objections.failure_scenario: A later change to pgstat snapshot or persistence code assumes fixed-amount kinds are small flat structs. It breaks the index-chained table, and no test outside stats.sql fails. Meanwhile every cluster allocates about 0.6 MiB of shared memory and writes it to the stats file at shutdown, even with track_log_messages = none.
objections.argument: Existing fixed-amount kinds such as archiver, bgwriter, io and wal are small fixed counters. Keyed data normally uses variable-numbered kinds in dshash. Message #5 keeps a bespoke hash table only because the fixed-amount memcpy snapshot rules out dshash, so pgstat would carry a second hashing scheme that only this feature uses. The table is also sized from the errcodes.txt count at compile time, so adding SQLSTATEs changes shared memory and the stats file size without anyone choosing to.
objections.author_must_show: Why can a variable-numbered kind, or a hybrid with a small fixed index, not hold these keys, and who keeps the custom table in sync with pgstat changes?

critic.reasoning: The author explains why dshash does not fit a fixed-amount kind, but not why a variable-numbered kind was not used. The 0.6 MiB allocated with tracking off is confirmed in message #5; the errcodes.txt part is covered by replication-ondisk-2.

objections.title: Counters silently depend on log_min_messages, a separate logging setting
objections.failure_scenario: A managed-platform operator raises log_min_messages to fatal, or sets it per role with alter role ... set, to cut log volume. track_log_messages = error stays on, but ERROR-level XX001 and XX000 are no longer counted for those sessions. The corruption alert from message #4 never fires, and nobody sees why until they read the docs.
objections.argument: Message #5 says log_min_messages acts as a floor on what is counted, so the meaning of track_log_messages depends on a second GUC that can differ per role and per database. Other track_* settings do not change meaning based on logging configuration. This coupling works against the use case in message #4, where monitoring should not depend on log access or log setup. Messages sent only to the client are never counted.
objections.author_must_show: Why should a statistics counter depend on log_min_messages instead of counting at error-report time, regardless of where the message goes?

critic.reasoning: Messages #1 and #5 state the log_min_messages floor but give no reason for it. A superuser can set log_min_messages per role or database, so the scenario can happen and conflicts with the alerting use case in message #4.

objections.title: One shared lock in EmitErrorReport() for every process, no numbers posted
objections.failure_scenario: A connection storm with a bad password makes hundreds of backends emit FATAL 28P01 at once. Each one takes the same LWLock to count, so authentication failures serialize and the error path slows down when the system is under the most stress. The postmaster also logs through this path and would wait on a shared-memory lock.
objections.argument: Message #1 states the counting takes one LWLock, and v2 moves this into EmitErrorReport() for all process types. The only measurement is a claim of low single-digit overhead in message #1, with no harness or numbers for either version. The postmaster normally avoids shared-memory locks so that it survives damaged shared state, and the proposal does not say how v2 handles that.
objections.author_must_show: What overhead do you measure with many concurrent backends logging, and does the postmaster or a backend in a critical section ever take the lock?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 confirms one LWLock per counted message and says the module handles the postmaster, without saying how. No harness or numbers are posted, so the concurrency and postmaster questions are open, though only for clusters that turn tracking on.

other_surviving.title: View column names depart from datid/datname/usesysid/usename convention
other_surviving.failure_scenario: If the column is named user, as the brief lists it, then `select user, count from pg_stat_log_messages` returns current_user on every row, because USER is a reserved SQL keyword. A dashboard author joins on database and user against pg_stat_activity and must write quoted identifiers and different names for the same data.
other_surviving.argument: Message #5 lists the columns as database and user, which it says are unchanged from v1, but the v1 docs use database_oid, database_name, user_oid and user_name. Neither set matches the datid, datname, usesysid and usename names in pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_database. A new core view becomes a permanent contract, so a committer would likely ask that it follow existing names and avoid reserved words.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What are the exact v2 column names, and why not reuse datid, datname, usesysid and usename as other pg_stat_* views do?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 lists database and user, the v1 docs use database_oid and user_name, and neither matches datid, datname, usesysid, usename. The `select user` scenario depends on the exact v2 names, which the material does not show, but the consistency question stands.

other_surviving.title: Stats block size tied to errcodes.txt without a format version check
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A developer adds a SQLSTATE to errcodes.txt and does not bump PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID. On the next clean restart the server reads the old fixed-size block with the new length, and the log-message entries and the records that follow it are misread. The stats may be silently wrong or rejected, and nothing in the errcode change warns the developer.
other_surviving.argument: Message #5 sizes the table at 64 entries per named errcode, generated from errcodes.txt, and the block is persisted verbatim. So the on-disk stats layout now changes whenever an errcode is added, which happens in many unrelated patches. Today a reviewer has no reason to look at the pgstat file format when reviewing a new errcode, so a missing format bump is easy to miss. The same risk applies to a minor release that backpatches an errcode.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What makes a stats file written with a different errcode count fail loudly on read, without depending on a manual PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID bump?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 confirms that the block size comes from the errcodes.txt count and that the block is persisted verbatim. The material names no check that catches a stats file written with a different errcode count.

other_surviving.title: Working extension already exists; core adds distribution, not capability
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An operator who can install extensions loads the existing pg_stat_log through shared_preload_libraries and gets the same per-SQLSTATE counters today. The core version counts the same messages, those that reach the server log, so it adds no new data. Every installation still carries the core code, a new GUC and about 0.6 MB of shared memory, even with tracking off.
other_surviving.argument: v1 runs as an out-of-tree extension on the custom cumulative statistics API, through emit_log_hook (messages #1 and #5). v2 moves counting into EmitErrorReport() but keeps log_min_messages as the floor, so it sees what the hook sees. Messages #4 and #5 argue for core because managed platforms are slow to add extensions and the preload requirement is inconvenient. A committer would likely ask whether these packaging and convenience reasons justify a permanent core stats kind when the extension already works.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What can the core stats kind count or guarantee that the existing extension, loaded through shared_preload_libraries, cannot?

critic.reasoning: Message #4 answers Daniel Gustafsson's question with distribution and access arguments, and v2 counts the same messages as the extension. Support comes from two people, one of whom worked on the extension, so the material does not yet show a common need.

refuted.title: Table size derived from errcodes.txt ties stats layout to SQLSTATE list
refuted.failure_scenario: A bug fix that adds an errcode is backpatched. The fixed-amount stats struct changes size in a minor release. After the minor update, the server reads a stats file written with the old layout and has to discard it or reject it, and that path is untested.
refuted.argument: Message #5 sizes the table as 64 entries per named errcode and embeds it in PgStat_ShmemControl and PgStat_Snapshot. Adding an SQLSTATE becomes a change to shared memory layout and to the stats file format, and a reviewer of an errcode patch is unlikely to notice. The proposal does not say how the stats file format id handles this.
refuted.author_must_show: What happens to the persisted stats file and shared memory layout when errcodes.txt gains an entry in a back branch?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-2, which states the same errcodes.txt layout coupling with a more exact failure path and also covers the back-branch case.

refuted.title: Crash recovery discards the counters the motivating alerts depend on
refuted.failure_scenario: A backend raises XX001 and then hits a PANIC, or any PANIC occurs. The postmaster restarts all processes and runs crash recovery, which discards the stats file and the shared counters. The monitoring system never sees the PANIC row or the late corruption errors, and the operator learns of them only from the log.
refuted.argument: Message #5 says the counters "are discarded after crash recovery, like other cumulative statistics". The view lists PANIC as an elevel, but a PANIC always ends in crash recovery, so its count cannot survive to be read. Message #4 justifies core placement by alerting on XX000, XX001 and XX002, which are the errors most likely to come just before a crash. The proposal does not say which of these events the view can report reliably.
refuted.author_must_show: Which severities and SQLSTATEs can the view report reliably when a crash follows them, and how will the documentation state that limit for PANIC?

critic.reasoning: Every cumulative statistics kind discards its counters after crash recovery, so the patch follows existing practice. Monitoring can detect a crash restart by other means, and what remains is a documentation note about PANIC rows, which is out of scope.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The stats file gains a block of about 0.6 MiB whose size follows the errcodes.txt count.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the system view pg_stat_log_messages and the function pg_stat_get_log_messages_dropped().

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a builtin stats kind, PGSTAT_KIND_LOGMSG, with its own hash table inside pgstat.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: The brief lists a view column named user, which is a reserved SQL keyword.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the enum GUC track_log_messages, default none.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Any role can raise errors that take slots in the shared table; reads need pg_read_all_stats.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: An errcode added in a back branch would change the shared memory and stats file layout.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Core would carry a new view, GUC, stats kind and a hash table used by this feature only.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Counting takes an LWLock in EmitErrorReport() for every tracked message in every process type.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: A working out-of-tree extension gives the same counters through emit_log_hook.

questions: How does the design keep XX000, XX001 and XX002 countable once the table is full, whether from many roles or from one role raising made-up SQLSTATEs?
Why can a variable-numbered stats kind, or the per-backend stats that Bertrand Drouvot suggested, not hold these keys?
Why does counting stop at the log_min_messages floor instead of counting at error-report time, wherever the message goes?
What overhead do you measure with many backends logging at once, and does the postmaster or a backend in a critical section take the lock?
What makes a stats file written with a different errcode count fail loudly on read, without a manual PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID bump?

committability.owner_note: The owner would need to know the cumulative statistics code and the error-reporting path in elog.c. Daniel Gustafsson commented on placement only, and nobody has reviewed v2 in detail.
committability.liability: A permanent core view and GUC, a stats file layout tied to errcodes.txt, and a lock taken in EmitErrorReport() by every process type, for as long as the view exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author rewrote the patch into core after message #3 and maintains the out-of-tree extension. The entry has needed a rebase since 2026-10-04.

priority.reason: Operators whose monitoring roles have no log access benefit, and the thread shows support. The capacity and stats-kind questions decide the shape of the patch, so detailed review should wait for them; review cost is an estimate because the v2 patch was not read.

provisional_note: The v2 patch text was not available, so the exact column names, the lock used, the postmaster handling and the GUC context could not be checked. Only the first three of six messages were shown in full.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: SQL statements statistics counter view (pg_stat_sql)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_sql view that counts SQL statements executed on the instance by command tag, behind a new track_sql GUC, with a reset function. Later versions keep one row per command tag in a hash table, counted in exec_simple_query and exec_execute_message.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback after months without activity, after Alvaro Herrera asked who would rebase it onto the new cmdtaglist.h enum tags. Andres Freund's 2017 review had left open questions: an extension might be the better place, tags should be enums in a fixed array, and counting belongs at the executor level. The author promised an array version, but the visible messages do not show one. A competing cmdstats patch by Mark Dilger also waited on benchmarks that Robert Haas requested.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch had no activity for months, so I am marking it as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Emit "checkpoint skipped because system is idle" message at LOG level if log_checkpoints is set
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Justin Pryzby, Kyotaro Horiguchi, Julien Rouhaud
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch raises the "checkpoint skipped because system is idle" message from DEBUG1 to LOG when log_checkpoints is set. The goal is to show in the server log that no checkpoints happened during idle periods.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Justin Pryzby argued that a message about doing nothing is a debug message, and that writing it can wake idle disks, for example through syslog fsync. He also noted that log_checkpoints became the default partly so that an idle instance would not write logs every 5 minutes. Kyotaro Horiguchi and Julien Rouhaud also voted -1 and suggested other ways to see skipped checkpoints, such as emit_log_hook or a counter in pg_stat_bgwriter. With no agreement, Justin Pryzby asked the author to close the CF entry, and it was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think it would be odd to write logs of increased severity, for the case where
we did not do anything.  I think it really is a debug log.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_logmsg
precedents_retrieved.summary: A new contrib extension, pg_stat_logmsg, modeled on pg_stat_statements, that counts emitted log messages in shared memory keyed by file name, line number and elevel. It also shows the format string, function name, sqlerrcode and later the version, so operators of many servers can find rare "should not happen" errors.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch did not change after September 2023. In July 2024 reviewers asked what blocked it, questioned whether it belongs in contrib, and pointed out that line numbers change between minor releases, so old and new entries mix after an upgrade. Michael Paquier suggested building on the proposed pluggable cumulative statistics instead of copying the pg_stat_statements design, which does not scale well. The author agreed to put the version in the key and to rework the patch, but said time was the main blocker, and the visible messages show no new version before the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The patch shares a lot of perks with pg_stat_statements that don't
scale well.

precedents_retrieved.title: transaction statistics of logical replication subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first proposed counting failed transactions and their sizes in pg_stat_replication_slots, so that users could tell successful logical decoding from repeated failed attempts. By the last version, the patch instead added apply_commit_count and apply_rollback_count columns to pg_stat_subscription_stats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila noted that pg_stat_database already shows committed and rolled-back transactions per database, so the new counters largely duplicate it, and he asked whether anyone saw value in them. Masahiko Sawada agreed that commit and rollback counts without transaction sizes no longer meet the original goal and have no concrete use case. The author then marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I’m concerned that adding only apply_commit_count
and apply_rollback_count ends up adding the duplicate statistics with
no concrete use cases.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix for REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW ownership error message
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW so that a permission failure reports "must be owner of materialized view" instead of the generic "must be owner of relation", by passing OBJECT_MATVIEW to the ACL check error path. The author offered to prepare back-patches for released branches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers considered the change cosmetic and argued against back-patching: the existing message is not wrong, and changing behavior in released branches can affect applications that depend on the current text. While writing a regression test, the author found that HEAD/v11 already produced the correct message because of an earlier commit. With no back-patch planned, nothing was left to fix, and the author withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As the plan is not to backpatch, I’ll withdraw my patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Track statistics for spilling of changes from ReorderBuffer".
precedents_retrieved.authors: Fujii Masao, Amit Kapila, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Track statistics for spilling of changes from ReorderBuffer".
Reverted commit(s): Don't call elog() while holding spinlock.; Doc: Update the documentation for spilled transaction statistics.; Fix unportable printf format introduced in commit 9290ad198.; Track statistics for spilling of changes from ReorderBuffer.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
The stats with this commit was available only for WALSenders, however,
users might want to see for backends doing logical decoding via SQL API.
Then, users might want to reset and access these stats across server
restart which was not possible with the current patch.

List of commits reverted:

caa3c4242c   Don't call elog() while holding spinlock.
e641b2a995   Doc: Update the documentation for spilled transaction
statistics.
5883f5fe27   Fix unportable printf format introduced in commit 9290ad198.
9290ad198b   Track statistics for spilling of changes from ReorderBuffer.

Additionaly, remove the release notes entry for this feature.

precedents_retrieved.title: Planning counters in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add planning counters to pg_stat_statements: a count of how many times a statement was planned and the total planning time, recorded through a planner hook alongside the existing execution counters. The patch passed the planning time to the executor through a new PlannedStmt field and had the planner hook bump the existing nesting level counter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the design: pgss_ExecutorEnd cleared a field in the cached PlannedStmt, which he said amounted to modifying the plan cache. He also questioned whether the planner hook should change nested_level, and he said the approach assumed a near one-to-one relationship between planner and executor calls that does not hold for cases such as prepared statements. He proposed having the planner hook record planning time with its own pgss_store() call. The author found that this needs the query text in the planner, which would mean changing function signatures, and returned the patch with feedback because he did not have time to rework it during the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
What we have here is pgss_ExecutorEnd stomping on the plan cache.
I do *not* find that acceptable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add parallel counters to pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add counters to pg_stat_statements that record how many times a statement was planned with parallelism and how many times it ran with parallel workers. A later version instead counted how often a parallel plan ran without any parallel workers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Julien Rouhaud said the counters cannot tell why a parallel plan ran without workers: the executor disabled parallel mode (!es_use_parallel_mode, as with the JDBC client) or no workers were free. He asked for separate counters for each case and for better column names. Nobody answered this review, and Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback after the thread had been idle for a few weeks.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Both situations are different and in my opinion require
different (and specialized) counters to properly handle them.

precedents_retrieved.title: Issue a log message when the backtrace logged is cut off
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes set_backtrace() in elog.c, and the backtrace code in assert.c, add a line such as "(backtrace limited to 100 frames)" when the backtrace reaches the buffer limit. It began as a documentation note about the 100-frame limit of backtrace_functions and changed to a log message at Peter Eisentraut's suggestion.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers supported the idea, but the last patch had open review points. On FreeBSD, backtrace() returned 99 frames, so the message never appeared. Yugo NAGATA noted that num_skip makes the reported count wrong, and Peter Eisentraut asked to print nframes and to test against lengthof(buf) - 1. No updated patch appears in the visible messages before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think this should actually print nframes, because that's the actual number of frames returned.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert error-throwing wrappers for the printf family of functions.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert error-throwing wrappers for the printf family of functions.
Reverted commit(s): Add error-throwing wrappers for the printf family of functions.; Permit use of vsprintf() in PostgreSQL code.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 16304a013432931e61e623c8d85e9fe24709d9ba, except
for its changes in src/port/snprintf.c; as well as commit
cac18a76bb6b08f1ecc2a85e46c9d2ab82dd9d23 which is no longer needed.

Fujii Masao reported that the previous commit caused failures in psql on
OS X, since if one exits the pager program early while viewing a query
result, psql sees an EPIPE error from fprintf --- and the wrapper function
thought that was reason to panic.  (It's a bit surprising that the same
does not happen on Linux.)  Further discussion among the security list
concluded that the risk of other such failures was far too great, and
that the one-size-fits-all approach to error handling embodied in the
previous patch is unlikely to be workable.

This leaves us again exposed to the possibility of the type of failure
envisioned in CVE-2015-3166.  However, that failure mode is strictly
hypothetical at this point: there is no concrete reason to believe that
an attacker could trigger information disclosure through the supposed
mechanism.  In the first place, the attack surface is fairly limited,
since so much of what the backend does with format strings goes through
stringinfo.c or psprintf(), and those already had adequate defenses.
In the second place, even granting that an unprivileged attacker could
control the occurrence of ENOMEM with some precision, it's a stretch to
believe that he could induce it just where the target buffer contains some
valuable information.  So we concluded that the risk of non-hypothetical
problems induced by the patch greatly outweighs the security risks.
We will therefore revert, and instead undertake closer analysis to
identify specific calls that may need hardening, rather than attempt a
universal solution.

We have kept the portion of the previous patch that improved snprintf.c's
handling of errors when it calls the platform's sprintf().  That seems to
be an unalloyed improvement.

roaster_notes.note: The closest precedent, pg_stat_logmsg [P3], which message #1 cites as its inspiration, was set aside over source-location keys that change between minor releases, a pg_stat_statements-style design and the contrib question. v2 answers each point: it uses stable SQLSTATE keys and the cumulative stats API, and moved into core after message #3. The missing benchmarks echo [P1], but that point belongs to the performance angle and rests only on an AI summary.
The proposal adds no WAL records, catalog changes or wire protocol changes. Its only persistent state is the cumulative stats file, so the objections above cover that file alone.

Read access through pg_read_all_stats and reset through pg_stat_reset_shared follow existing practice. The material does not say whether track_log_messages is superuser-only, so that point is left as a question.
Objections listed; the idea itself has demand in messages #2 and #4.

One objection only. pg_stat_database counts deadlocks, rollbacks, conflicts and checksum failures but has no general SQLSTATE counter, so this objection rests on the existing extension, not on core views.

The material shows real demand that has lasted. The 2023 pg_stat_logmsg proposal [P3], this author and three thread participants want error counters, and message #4 gives a concrete alerting case (XX000/XX001/XX002) for managed setups where monitoring roles get pg_monitor but not log access. Cost falls mostly on users because counting is off by default, apart from the 0.6 MB of shared memory and stats file space that every instance pays.
